name: Analogy (qiyās)
definition: Carrying a rule from what was heard over to what was not, because the two share the reason for the rule: the second source of grammar after samāʿ.
body: The grammarians' analogy has four parts, as Ibn al-Anbārī sets them out on the model of legal analogy: the base (aṣl), the case it is extended to (farʿ), the cause they share (ʿilla) and the ruling (ḥukm). Because the Arabs were heard putting the doer in rafʿ, every doer is put in rafʿ, including those in words the Arabs never said.

Ibn Abī Isḥāq, al-Zubaydī reports, was the first to stretch analogy, and the Basrans held it more strictly than the Kufans: what goes against it they called shādhdh, explained away (taʾwīl) or put down to the needs of verse (ḍarūra). The saying 'grammar is analogy that is followed' (al-naḥw qiyās yuttabaʿ) is quoted in many books.

examples.text: Every doer is in rafʿ: a rule heard in the speech of the Arabs and extended by analogy to every doer.
